en: To tolerate; to accept or act in accordance with a rule
hook: ABIDE: can't ABIDE it = can't stand it. ABIDE BY = obey.
story: Abide. To tolerate something; also, to accept or obey a rule, as in abide by. Faisal's university hostel in Rajshahi had one strict rule: lights out at eleven. Faisal abided by it without complaint. What he could not abide was his roommate's snoring, loud as a passing truck. After a week of sleepless nights, he [chuckle] bought earplugs at the market and finally slept. The trick: if you abide by a rule, you obey it; if you cannot abide something, you cannot stand it. So, what verb means to obey, or, with not, to be unable to bear something? ... Abide.

gre.s: A meticulous editor, she could not ____ even minor errors of punctuation, and she returned any manuscript that contained them without reading further.
gre.clue: returned any manuscript that contained them

example: Grandmother cannot abide wasted food, so leftover rice in her kitchen always reappears the next morning as panta bhat.

en: To stay stuck to something; to keep faithfully to a rule or belief
hook: ADHERE: like ADHESIVE tape.
story: Adhere. To stick firmly to something; also, to stay faithful to a rule or belief. Sanjida's father worked as a clerk in a government office in Cumilla for thirty years. People often offered him gifts to move their files faster: sweets, saris, once even a goat. He refused every one. He adhered to his principles, even when money at home was tight. Sanjida grew up proud of a father who adhered to the truth. Adhere shares its root with adhesive, like tape that stays stuck. So, what verb means to stick firmly to a rule or belief? ... Adhere.

gre.s: Although the committee claimed to ____ to the principle of transparency, it conducted most of its deliberations behind closed doors and published no minutes.
gre.clue: it conducted most of its deliberations behind closed doors

example: The bakery adheres strictly to its founder's recipe, using no preservatives and baking every loaf by hand before dawn.

en: To make changes in order to improve or correct
hook: AMEND: MEND something to make it better.
story: Amend. To change something in order to improve or correct it. In Rubel's neighbourhood in Khulna, the playground committee had an old rule: only boys could use the field. When a group of girls kept turning up with a borrowed cricket bat, Rubel's mother asked the committee to think again. After a long meeting, they amended the rule. Now girls play on Friday mornings, and they are winning. Mend is actually a shortened form of amend: to amend something is to mend it. So, what verb means to change a rule or text to improve it? ... Amend.

gre.s: Faced with mounting evidence of its flaws, the legislature voted to ____ the law rather than repeal it entirely.
gre.clue: rather than repeal it entirely

example: After readers pointed out several errors, the newspaper amended the article and printed a correction on its front page.

en: Able to express ideas clearly and effectively; to express clearly
hook: ARTICULATE: every ARTICLE of speech placed perfectly.
story: Articulate. Able to express ideas clearly; as a verb, to express clearly. Kona came from a small town in Lalmonirhat to a job interview in Dhaka, her hands shaking. Then they asked why she wanted to work in public health. She spoke about her mother's village clinic, the queue of women at dawn, and her plan to train local health workers. Her words were calm and clear. Afterwards, the panel praised how articulate she was. Articulate comes from the Latin for a small joint: articulate speech is clearly jointed, each part distinct. So, what word describes someone who expresses ideas clearly? ... Articulate.

gre.s: Although the witness was only fourteen, her testimony was remarkably ____, laying out the events in clear, precise sentences that impressed even the hostile lawyers.
gre.clue: laying out the events in clear, precise sentences

example: Shy at home, Tahmina became remarkably articulate in front of a microphone, and her radio show soon had listeners across Rajshahi.

en: A standard against which things are measured
hook: BENCHMARK: a mark on the workbench to measure against.
story: Benchmark. A standard against which other things are measured. Every sweet yogurt Tareq has ever tasted, he compares with his grandmother's mishti doi in Bogura, set in a clay pot until it is thick enough to hold a spoon upright. Restaurants in Dhaka try, but none comes close. [sigh] For the whole family, her yogurt is the benchmark. Benchmark began as a surveyor's mark carved into stone, a fixed point for measuring heights. A benchmark is the fixed point you measure everything else against. So, what word means the standard others are compared with? ... Benchmark.

gre.s: For decades, the textbook's rigorous treatment of the subject served as the ____ against which all later introductions were judged, and few of them measured up.
gre.clue: against which all later introductions were judged

example: Ten seconds for the hundred metres remains the benchmark that separates good sprinters from truly great ones.

en: Bringing sudden, terrible harm or ruin
hook: CATASTROPHIC: a CATASTROPHE.
story: Catastrophic. Causing sudden, terrible harm or ruin. In November two thousand seven, Cyclone Sidr struck the southwest coast of Bangladesh. Winds tore down homes, a storm surge swept across villages, and thousands of lives were lost. For families in Barguna and Bagerhat, the damage was catastrophic. Since then, more shelters and early warnings have saved countless lives in later storms. Catastrophic comes from catastrophe, the Greek word for an overturning: a catastrophic event turns life upside down. So, what word describes a disaster that brings sudden and terrible ruin? ... Catastrophic.

gre.s: Engineers warned that even a small crack in the aging dam could prove ____, releasing a flood that would drown every village in the valley below.
gre.clue: releasing a flood that would drown every village in the valley below

example: A single typo in the guidance software had catastrophic results, sending the rocket off course seconds after takeoff.

en: Intellectual rather than emotional or physical; related to the brain
hook: CEREBRAL = cerebrum, the thinking part of the brain.
story: Cerebral. Intellectual rather than emotional; also, relating to the brain. On Friday nights, Laila wants old Bangla films where everyone cries at the end. Her brother Nadim wants cerebral films about time loops, memory and puzzles that he explains for an hour afterwards. Their mother [laugh] settles it by making them alternate weeks. Laila says Nadim's films have no heart; Nadim says they make you think. The cerebrum is the thinking part of the brain, so cerebral things appeal to the mind. So, what word describes something intellectual rather than emotional? ... Cerebral.

gre.s: Critics who expected a stirring, emotional drama found the film disappointingly ____, more interested in testing the audience's logic than in moving its heart.
gre.clue: more interested in testing the audience's logic than in moving its heart

example: Chess may be a cerebral game, but grandmasters train their bodies too, since a six-hour match is physically exhausting.

en: A loose sleeveless coat; something that hides; to hide or disguise
hook: CLOAK: like an invisibility cloak, hiding the truth.
story: Cloak. A loose outer coat; also, something that hides; as a verb, to hide or disguise. On winter mornings at the ferry ghat in Paturia, a thick fog cloaks the Padma. You cannot see the river, the boats, or even the far end of the jetty. Only the low horn of a ferry tells Nayan that it is out there somewhere. By ten, the sun burns through, and the cloak lifts. Picture an invisibility cloak: whatever it covers simply disappears. So, what verb means to cover something so it cannot be seen? ... Cloak.

gre.s: The regime tried to ____ its crackdown in the language of public safety, describing mass arrests as routine precautions.
gre.clue: describing mass arrests as routine precautions

example: Morning fog cloaked the Jamuna so thickly that the ferry crew had to sound the horn every few minutes.

en: To begin
hook: COMMENCE: COMMENCEMENT is when graduates BEGIN their new life.
story: Commence. To begin. The hall at Pushpita's HSC exam centre in Jessore fell silent. Two hundred students sat with pens ready, hearts pounding. The invigilator looked at the clock and announced, "The examination will now commence." Papers rustled, [sigh] and Pushpita took a deep breath and wrote her name. Months of night study had led to this moment, and now it had commenced. Think of a commencement ceremony at a university: graduates are not ending, but commencing a new life. So, what formal verb means to begin? ... Commence.

gre.s: Although the ceremony was scheduled to ____ at nine, the chief guest's late arrival meant that nothing actually happened until nearly noon.
gre.clue: nothing actually happened until nearly noon

example: Construction of the new bridge will commence as soon as the rainy season ends and the river falls.

en: Combining so as to complete or enhance each other
hook: COMPLEMENTARY with an E COMPLETES. Complimentary with an I means free or praising.
story: Complementary. Combining to complete or improve each other. Fahim and Ananya run a tiny bakery in Sylhet. Fahim wakes at four to bake bread and cakes, but he hates talking to customers. Ananya cannot bake at all, but she remembers every customer's name and keeps the accounts perfectly. Alone, each would struggle. Together, their complementary skills make the bakery the busiest on the street. Complementary with an e completes; complimentary with an i means free or full of praise. So, what word describes two things that complete each other? ... Complementary.

gre.s: The two researchers' skills proved ____: her expertise in statistics filled exactly the gaps in his knowledge of biology.
gre.clue: filled exactly the gaps in his knowledge

example: Rice and lentils are nutritionally complementary, since each supplies amino acids that the other lacks.

en: To argue or assert something; to struggle against difficulties
bn: দাবি করা; প্রতিদ্বন্দ্বিতা বা মোকাবেলা করা
hook: CONTEND: CONTENDERs fight in a competition; scholars contend in arguments.
story: Contend. To struggle against a difficulty; also, to argue that something is true. In the Barind region near Rajshahi, farmers contend with hard red soil, fierce heat and a falling water table. Robiul has farmed there all his life, watching the wells go deeper every year. His daughter, now a researcher, contends that farmers should switch to crops that need less water. Slowly, some are listening. A contender is someone who contends, struggling to win a contest. So, what verb means to struggle with difficulties, or to argue a point? ... Contend.

gre.s: Some economists ____ that the recession was caused by excessive regulation, while others argue that deregulation was to blame.
gre.clue: while others argue

example: The defense contends that the security video was recorded on a different night, and it has asked an expert to examine the timestamps.

en: Not openly shown; secret
hook: COVERT: kept under COVER.
story: Covert. Secret; not openly shown. For eleven years, Saiful's mother kept a covert savings plan. Every week, she slipped a few coins and folded notes into a clay money bank hidden behind the rice sacks. Nobody knew. When Saiful got into university in Chattogram, she broke the clay bank in front of him, and coins rolled across the floor. [gasp] Her covert savings bought his first laptop. Covert comes from the same root as cover: something covert is kept under cover. Its opposite is overt, meaning open. So, what word describes something done in secret? ... Covert.

gre.s: Unlike his opponent's openly hostile campaign, the senator's attacks were ____, conducted through anonymous leaks and rumors spread by intermediaries.
gre.clue: conducted through anonymous leaks and rumors

example: The journalist used a covert camera hidden in a pen to film inspectors accepting bribes at the port.

en: Causing harm or damage
hook: DETRIMENTAL: leads to DETRIMENT (harm).
story: Detrimental. Causing harm or damage. During her exam month, Antara studied until midnight, then lay in bed scrolling her phone until three. Every morning she woke with a heavy head and read the same page four times. Her doctor aunt finally told her that late-night scrolling was detrimental to her sleep, and poor sleep was detrimental to her memory. Antara left the phone in the kitchen that night. Detriment means harm; it comes from the Latin for rubbing away, as harm slowly rubs you down. So, what word describes a habit that causes damage? ... Detrimental.

gre.s: Although the pesticide boosted crop yields in the short term, it proved ____ to the region's bees, whose populations collapsed within a few years.
gre.clue: whose populations collapsed within a few years

example: Heavy pumping of groundwater has proved detrimental to Dhaka's soil, which is slowly sinking in several neighborhoods.

en: To give orders with authority; to control or determine
hook: DICTATE: what a DICTATOR does.
story: Dictate. To give orders with authority; also, to control or determine something. In the haor wetlands of Sunamganj, water dictates everything. For half the year, villages become islands, and people travel only by boat. In the dry months, the same water turns into rice fields as far as the eye can see. When to plant, when to harvest, even when to hold weddings: the water dictates it all. A dictator dictates orders; here, nature is the one in charge. So, what verb means to control or determine what happens? ... Dictate.

gre.s: The tiny budget seemed to ____ every decision the filmmakers made, from the choice of actors to the length of each scene.
gre.clue: from the choice of actors to the length of each scene

example: In the end, the weather will dictate whether the farmers of Dinajpur plant wheat or maize this winter.

en: To disagree with an official or widely held opinion
hook: DIS-SENT: DIS-agree with the SENTiment.
story: Dissent. To disagree with an official or widely held view; as a noun, that disagreement. At a family meeting in Pabna, eleven relatives agreed to sell the ancestral pond to a developer for a good price. Only one voice dissented: Nayan's grandmother. She said the pond had fed three generations and would feed three more. Her dissent made everyone pause. In the end, they kept the pond. Dissent comes from the Latin for feeling differently, the same root as in sentiment. So, what word means disagreeing with what most people have decided? ... Dissent.

gre.s: Although most of the committee endorsed the proposal enthusiastically, two members chose to ____, arguing that its costs had been badly underestimated.
gre.clue: arguing that its costs had been badly underestimated

example: When the board approved the merger, only one director dissented, warning that thousands of workers would lose their jobs.

en: Suffering from anxiety, sorrow, or pain; in serious difficulty
hook: DISTRESSED: under heavy STRESS.
story: Distressed. Suffering from anxiety, sorrow or pain; also, in serious difficulty. At a crowded Boishakhi fair in Rangpur, four-year-old Mim let go of her father's hand to look at the balloons. When she turned back, he was gone. She stood frozen, crying, deeply distressed. A tea seller lifted her onto his counter and asked the loudspeaker man to call her father. Ten minutes later, her father pushed through the crowd and held her tight. Stress is actually a shortened form of distress: a distressed person is under heavy stress. So, what word describes someone filled with fear or sorrow? ... Distressed.

gre.s: Hotline volunteers are trained to calm ____ callers, many of whom are panicking or in tears when they first phone in.
gre.clue: many of whom are panicking or in tears

example: The lifeguard spotted a distressed swimmer waving near the rocks and reached him moments before he went under.

en: Unconventional and slightly strange
hook: EC-CENTRIC: off-center, not in the middle like everyone else.
story: Eccentric. Unconventional and slightly strange. In a lane in Old Dhaka lives an old man who wears a yellow raincoat every single day, even in the dry heat of April. He talks to the potted plants on his balcony and greets each one by name. Children once laughed at him, but he gives free English lessons every evening, and now half the lane calls him teacher. He is eccentric, and deeply loved. Eccentric means off centre, from Greek: an eccentric person lives a little away from the middle. So, what word describes someone pleasantly odd and unconventional? ... Eccentric.

gre.s: The billionaire was known for his ____ habits, such as wearing a raincoat indoors and dining only on food that was blue.
gre.clue: wearing a raincoat indoors and dining only on food that was blue

example: The eccentric poet kept a pet goose on his rooftop in Old Dhaka and read his new verses to it every evening.

en: To persuade; to bring about or cause
hook: INDUCE: lead (duce) INTO.
story: Induce. To persuade someone to do something; also, to cause something. Mehjabin could not induce her little brother to eat bitter gourd. He clamped his mouth shut every time. Then their grandmother told him that bitter gourd was the secret food of famous fast bowlers. That evening he ate a whole plate, [laugh] and asked for more. Grandmother had induced him with a story. Induce comes from the Latin ducere, to lead, as in conductor: to induce is to lead someone into doing something. So, what verb means to persuade or bring about? ... Induce.

gre.s: No amount of flattery could ____ the reclusive author to grant an interview; she had refused every request from journalists for over thirty years.
gre.clue: she had refused every request from journalists for over thirty years

example: The company offered free mobile data to induce farmers to try its new weather app before the planting season.

en: Based on instinct rather than conscious reasoning; easy to understand without instruction
hook: INTUITIVE: you just KNOW, by INTUITION.
story: Intuitive. Based on instinct rather than conscious reasoning; also, easy to use without instructions. Tahsin called his mother in Noakhali from his hostel in Dhaka and said, "Everything is fine, Ma." She was quiet for a moment, then asked, "Who has upset you?" He had said nothing, but she knew. A mother's understanding is intuitive. Within five minutes he was telling her everything. Intuitive comes from intuition, knowing something without being told. So, what word describes understanding that comes from instinct, not reasoning? ... Intuitive.

gre.s: Rather than calculating the odds, the veteran player relied on an ____ sense of when to attack, a feel for the game that she could never fully explain.
gre.clue: a feel for the game that she could never fully explain

example: Experienced nurses often have an intuitive feel for which patient is about to get worse, long before the monitors show it.

en: Freedom to act or decide as one chooses
hook: LATITUDE: lots of room, wide like LATITUDE lines across the globe.
story: Latitude. Freedom to act or decide as one chooses. Most art teachers at Nipa's school in Dinajpur gave strict instructions: draw a village scene, a boat, or the national flag. But the new teacher gave her students latitude. "Paint anything that matters to you." Nipa painted her grandmother's wrinkled hands holding a cup of tea. With that latitude, she found her own style. Latitude comes from the Latin for wide: the lines of latitude run across the width of the globe, and latitude gives you wide room. So, what word means freedom to choose your own way? ... Latitude.

gre.s: The new editor gave her reporters considerable ____, allowing them to pursue whatever stories interested them rather than assigning topics herself.
gre.clue: rather than assigning topics herself

example: Judges have some latitude in sentencing, so two people convicted of the same crime may receive very different punishments.

en: Not strict or careful enough
hook: LAX: think RELAXED rules.
story: Lax. Not strict or careful enough. The guard at Bappy's apartment building in Uttara was a kind man, but very lax. He dozed through the afternoon heat, let delivery men in without asking, and left the gate open at night. Then one morning, three bicycles were missing from the garage. After that, the residents set up a sign-in book, and nobody called the building lax again. Lax and relaxed come from the same Latin word for loose: lax rules are far too loose. So, what word describes security that is careless and not strict enough? ... Lax.

gre.s: The audit blamed the fraud on ____ oversight, noting that no one had reviewed the accounts in over three years.
gre.clue: no one had reviewed the accounts in over three years

example: Parents complained that the school was lax about homework, since some teachers had not set any for an entire term.

en: Producing a great deal of profit
hook: LUCRATIVE: brings in lots of LUCRE (money).
story: Lucrative. Producing a lot of profit. Deepa learned graphic design from free videos on a second-hand laptop in Rangpur. At first, she earned a few dollars making logos for small shops abroad. Within three years, clients from five countries were sending her work, and she was earning more than her father ever had. Freelancing had turned out to be lucrative. Lucrative comes from lucre, an old word for money, from the Latin for profit. So, what word describes work that brings in a lot of money? ... Lucrative.

gre.s: Many talented scientists abandon research for more ____ careers in finance, where salaries can be ten times higher.
gre.clue: where salaries can be ten times higher

example: Exporting frozen shrimp has become a lucrative trade for farmers in Satkhira, though it has also made their land saltier.

en: To make something less severe, serious, or painful
hook: MITIGATE: put MITTENS on the GATE — softens the blow.
story: Mitigate. To make something less severe or painful. When Cyclone Sidr struck in two thousand seven, the Sundarbans mangrove forest took the first blow. Its thick roots and dense trees broke the force of the wind and the waves before they reached many villages. Ashraf, a forest guard, says the forest is like a wall of green. The mangroves did not stop the storm, but they mitigated its damage. Mitigate comes from the Latin mitis, meaning soft or mild: to mitigate is to soften. So, what verb means to make harm less severe? ... Mitigate.

gre.s: Planting mangroves along the coast can ____ the impact of storm surges, though it cannot prevent them entirely.
gre.clue: though it cannot prevent them entirely

example: Wide, tree-lined avenues help mitigate the heat of a city summer by shading the pavements and cooling the air.

en: Very small, far below real value; existing in name only
hook: NOMINAL: in NAME only (nomen).
story: Nominal. Very small, far below the real value; also, existing in name only. The little library in Mukta's village in Jhenaidah charges a nominal fee: five taka a month. For that, children can borrow any book on the shelves. The librarian, a retired teacher, says the fee is only nominal, just enough to make children feel the books are truly theirs. Nominal comes from the Latin nomen, name: a nominal fee is a fee in name only. So, what word describes a cost so small that it is almost symbolic? ... Nominal.

gre.s: Although she was the ____ chair of the committee, real authority rested with her deputy, who set the agenda and made every major decision.
gre.clue: real authority rested with her deputy

example: The king remained the nominal ruler of the country, but parliament had long since taken over every real decision.

en: To prove stronger; to be widespread
hook: PRE-VAIL: PREVALENT and victorious.
story: Prevail. To prove stronger and win; also, to be widespread. On sports day at a school in Feni, the girls' tug of war team faced a much bigger team. Everyone expected them to lose. But they had practised together all month, pulling in rhythm to a chant. Slowly, step by step, the rope moved their way, [gasp] and the bigger team tumbled over. Teamwork had prevailed. Prevail and prevalent share a Latin root meaning to be stronger. So, what verb means to win in the end, against the odds? ... Prevail.

gre.s: Though the reformers were outnumbered and underfunded, their persistence allowed them to ____ in the end, and the law they had championed passed by a wide margin.
gre.clue: the law they had championed passed by a wide margin

example: After a fierce debate, common sense prevailed, and the council agreed to keep the old banyan tree instead of widening the road.

en: Having unusual or peculiar habits or features
hook: QUIRKY: full of QUIRKS, odd little habits.
story: Quirky. Having unusual habits or features that are odd in a charming way. Rony's uncle in Kishoreganj names every cow after a Bangla poet. There is a Nazrul who kicks, a Jibanananda who stares at the sky, and a gentle little calf named Sukanta. He also plays old film songs to them every evening, saying it improves the milk. Neighbours think he is quirky. Rony thinks he is the best uncle in the world. Quirky simply means full of quirks, odd little habits. So, what word describes someone with charmingly unusual habits? ... Quirky.

gre.s: Fans love the director's ____ films, which feature talking furniture, symmetrical sets, and characters who speak only in rhyme.
gre.clue: talking furniture, symmetrical sets, and characters who speak only in rhyme

example: The quirky little bookshop in Nilkhet arranges its novels by the colour of their covers rather than by author.

en: Spreading unchecked; widespread and uncontrolled
hook: RAMPANT: RAMPAGING everywhere.
story: Rampant. Spreading without control; widespread. One evening, a rumour spread across Dhaka on social media: salt was about to run out. By night, panic buying was rampant. Shampa saw people at the corner shop carrying away five, ten, even twenty packets. Prices shot up. The next day, officials announced there was plenty of salt, and the panic faded as quickly as it had begun. In old coats of arms, a lion rampant rears up on its hind legs, wild and unstoppable. So, what word describes something spreading wildly out of control? ... Rampant.

gre.s: In the absence of any regulatory oversight, fraud became ____ in the industry, spreading so widely that honest firms struggled to compete.
gre.clue: spreading so widely that honest firms struggled to compete

example: Weeds grew rampant in the abandoned garden, and within two summers they had swallowed the path to the front door.

en: No longer needed; unnecessary repetition
hook: REDUNDANT: RE-DONE, repeated without need.
story: Redundant. Unnecessary because it repeats something; also, no longer needed. Mukta proudly gave her essay to her editor. It began, "In my own personal opinion, I personally think." Her editor [chuckle] crossed out five words and left only "I think." "Own, personal and opinion are all redundant here," he said. "I think already says it." Mukta laughed and started cutting every redundant word in her essay. Redundant comes from the Latin for overflowing, like a wave spilling over: more than is needed. So, what word describes words that repeat without adding anything? ... Redundant.

gre.s: Because the new software performs all of its checks automatically, the old manual inspections have become ____, and the company plans to eliminate them next year.
gre.clue: the company plans to eliminate them next year

example: Once every train was fitted with automatic doors, the guard who used to stand at each carriage became redundant.

en: Existing only on the surface; lacking depth
hook: SUPER-FICIAL: only on the SURFACE (super = above).
story: Superficial. Existing only on the surface; lacking depth. A glamorous new restaurant opened in Banani, with chandeliers, gold-painted walls and waiters in bow ties. Ibrahim and his friends waited an hour for a table. Then the food came: cold rice, bland curry and dry chicken. [sigh] They left hungry. All its charm was superficial. Superficial comes from Latin super, above, and facies, face: it stays on the face of things, never going deeper. So, what word describes something impressive only on the surface? ... Superficial.

gre.s: Reviewers faulted the biography as ____, noting that it catalogued its subject's achievements without ever probing his motives or inner life.
gre.clue: without ever probing his motives or inner life

example: A superficial reading of the poem suggests a simple love story, but a closer look reveals a protest against the war.

en: Cautious and alert about possible danger or problems
hook: WARY sounds like WORRY: you worry, so you're careful.
story: Wary. Cautious and alert to possible danger. Every spring, honey collectors enter the Sundarbans in small groups. They move slowly through the mangroves, watching the mud for paw prints and listening for the slightest sound. A Bengal tiger could be hiding anywhere. Old Ibrahim tells the young men that only the wary come home. Wary shares its root with beware and aware. Do not confuse it with weary, which means tired. So, what word describes someone cautious and watchful of danger? ... Wary.

gre.s: Having been misled by flattering forecasts before, the investors were ____ of the startup's promise to triple its revenue within a year.
gre.clue: Having been misled by flattering forecasts before

example: Having been badly stung once, the village beekeeper is wary of opening the hives without his net and gloves.
